native_result.query: In what centuries did we see the highest growth phase of the period between 2000 BCE and 1100 BCE?
native_result.HypoA: Between 1500 BCE and 1300 BCE, highest growth of the period between 2000 BCE and 1100 BCE is seen.
native_result.HypoB: The highest growth phase of 2000-1100 BCE occurred in the 15th century BCE (1500-1401 BCE), extending into the 14th century BCE: all three growth tracks (archaeological find density, material-culture capital index, and pollen-based land-use openness) peak in the 15th century BCE, with the 14th century BCE sustaining demographic and land-use growth but not material-culture growth; decline follows in the 13th-12th centuries BCE.
native_result.WorkflowB: Verified data coverage (901 continuous annual rows per file in CE -2000..-1100; capital.csv is the exact 100-year-grain source of the 12 Z indicators; ts.pollen == Belau_PC1). Defined centuries as N000-N001 BCE. Track a: per-century mean/cumulative g_all_mean and endpoint log-difference of kde_all_mean (yearly grain). Track b: century-over-century DeltaZ for 12 indicators, mean DeltaZ, count increasing, and DeltaPC1 of a PCA composite from capital.csv at native grain (_inter columns only as robustness). Track c: per-century mean pollen_grate_100, Delta pollen_inter_100, Delta SMOOTH_MEAN_100y, and raw-observation counts. Ranked per metric, averaged ranks for triangulation, and ran a 1-year boundary-shift sensitivity check. Sign convention: g_all_mean and pollen_grate_100 are per-year fractional rates, positive = increase. Limitations: 94.7% of pollen values in-window are interpolated (5-6 raw points per century); KDE growth partly reflects sampling-density bias; the 11th century BCE (1100-1001) lies almost entirely outside the window so peaks are ranked among the 20th-12th centuries BCE.

sub_hypo.text: Within 2000–1100 BCE, the highest growth phase occurred in the 15th century BCE (1500–1401 BCE), extending into the 14th century BCE: archaeological find density, material-culture capital, and pollen-based land-use openness all peak in growth in the 15th century BCE; demographic and land-use growth, but not material-culture growth, persist in the 14th century BCE, followed by decline in the 13th–12th centuries BCE.
sub_hypo.context: Archaeological and pollen time series covering CE -2000 through -1100, with 901 continuous annual rows and capital indicators sourced at native 100-year grain. Century-level peaks are ranked among the 20th–12th centuries BCE because the 11th century lies almost entirely outside the window. Rankings are triangulated across metrics and checked with a one-year boundary shift; interpolated capital columns serve only as robustness checks. Interpretation is limited by possible KDE sampling-density bias and by 94.7% of in-window pollen values being interpolated, with only 5–6 raw observations per century.
sub_hypo.relations: A shared temporal maximum in growth, not necessarily in indicator levels, occurs in the 15th century BCE across all three tracks. Find-density growth is assessed using century mean/cumulative g_all_mean and endpoint log-differences of kde_all_mean; capital growth using century-over-century changes in the 12 Z indicators, their mean change, the count increasing, and change in their PCA composite; land-use growth using mean pollen_grate_100 and changes in pollen_inter_100 and SMOOTH_MEAN_100y. Positive g_all_mean and pollen_grate_100 denote increases. The subsequent pattern is track-specific: demographic and land-use growth persist in the 14th century BCE, whereas capital growth does not; decline follows in the 13th–12th centuries BCE.
